idiom_name: two-channel router + external toggle (control channel/config) + two outcome-equivalent legs
implementation_notes:
Language-neutral form: keep exactly one delivery step to the destination and put the extra stage(s) behind a single predicate that is set from outside the message — a control channel, a configuration service, a feature flag (LaunchDarkly, Unleash), or an operational flag. The predicate selects between the direct leg (unmodified message to the destination) and the detour leg (message through validation/testing/debugging steps, then to the same destination). Never read the toggle from the payload: an in-message flag turns the Detour into a Content-Based Router that any producer can steer. Keep the detour steps' failure policy explicit (fail the message or fall back to the direct leg) and make the enabled state observable so operators can tell which leg a message took. In service mesh environments, Istio VirtualService fault injection and Envoy BackendTrafficPolicy are declarative Detour implementations that require no application code changes.

Service-mesh realization: In Istio, a VirtualService with fault injection rules is a runtime Detour: the fault (delay or abort) is the detour step, applied conditionally via header matching (e.g., x-chaos-test: true) or weight-based routing. Envoy Gateway's BackendTrafficPolicy exposes fault injection as a CRD attached to HTTPRoute. Neither requires application code changes — the sidecar proxy handles the detour transparently. This is the modern cloud-native form of the Detour pattern where the 'toggle' is the VirtualService/Policy applied via kubectl.
code_sketch:
route(message):
    if toggle.enabled:                 # control channel / config / feature flag; NEVER the payload
        message = detour_steps(message)  # inspect and/or modify in place
    return destination(message)        # same destination on both legs
pitfalls: Letting the establishment of the toggle be implicit (an environment variable read once at start) instead of an auditable control operation.
Two separate delivery calls — one per leg — which drift apart until the switched-on path breaks.
Leaving a debugging detour permanently enabled, so full payloads are dumped in production.
A detour that fails silently and falls back to the direct leg without alerting, masking downstream failures.
Stacking multiple detours in series until the routing graph becomes unreadable and order guarantees are lost.

Wrong move: leaving the detour toggle in place long after its purpose is served -> stale toggles pile up as flag debt (a scan of 1,900 public repos found stale flags averaging ~14 months, 46% over a year) and the unexercised detour leg rots until the day it is switched on and fails -> instead give every detour an expiry date and removal ticket, and delete the toggle and its branch once the goal is met.

Wrong move: pointing a mirrored detour leg at a destination that performs side effects (DB writes, payments, emails) -> duplicated business outcomes or feedback loops when shadow responses leak back into the primary flow -> instead keep the detour destination a side-effect-free clone or observer, and never feed its responses back.

Wrong move: driving the detour from a request header any client can set (x-mirror-cluster, x-chaos-test) without access control -> external callers steer production traffic into fault-injection or debug paths -> instead derive the toggle from operator-controlled config, or restrict header-driven activation to authenticated, trusted traffic.
